name: Lena Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you say stays confidential and won't be traced back to you. Could you begin by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the store replenishment team at Marlowe Supermarkets head office. There are eight of us, and we decide how much of everything each of 140 stores gets, from milk to barbecue charcoal. The software suggests the orders, and my planners check them and fix the ones that are clearly wrong, like sending 200 bags of charcoal to a store when rain is forecast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle and the people. My planners are a good bunch and we eat lunch together most days. What tires me out is public holidays and heatwaves, when everything goes wrong at once and the store managers ring me directly. I'm 27, married to Karim, who's a field engineer at the water company, and we bought a small house last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a quiet relief. Our ordering software already uses some kind of AI, and it still can't tell a heatwave from a normal week without one of my planners checking. If it stays like that, my team's needed for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we were right to keep people checking the numbers. At work I'd be the sensible one saying the tools help but don't replace judgement. With family I'd say it was all a lot of noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pleased, mostly for my team. Two of them are supporting their parents and I'd hate to see them lose out. For me, it means I can plan a family without a big question mark over my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and ask for a training budget so my planners get better with the software we've got. Karim and I would keep to our plan of trying for a baby in about two years. And I'd keep putting a fifth of my salary into savings like we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and settled. Grateful, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the software can't spot a heatwave. Tell me about a time it got it wrong.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last August it ordered normal ice cream amounts for the coastal stores during the hottest week of the year. We caught it on the Sunday, and Daniyal on my team stayed late to fix about 30 stores by hand. Without him, those freezers would have been empty by Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else weighing on you at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marlowe's had a tough year, prices are high and customers are switching to the discount chains. There's talk of trimming head office, but not my team, because we're the ones who stop waste. So no, not really.

say: We were **right to keep people** checking the numbers.
The tools help but **don't replace judgement**.
With family I'd say it was all **a lot of noise**.
think: I'd be **pleased for my team**, two of whom support their parents.
I could **plan a family** without a question mark over my job.
do: Ask for a **training budget** so planners use current software better.
Keep saving **a fifth** of my salary.
Stick to **trying for a baby** in about two years.
S0.quote: Our ordering software already uses some kind of AI, and it still can't tell a heatwave from a normal week without one of my planners checking.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on **checking work** the software still can't do, like heatwave orders.
She thinks of **team members** supporting parents before herself.
Marlowe's **tough year** worries her little, since her team prevents waste.

steps.text: Ask for a training budget for the planners on current software
Keep saving a fifth of my salary each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying, that's us. If the software gets good enough to plan orders properly, eight planners becomes three, and maybe the three report to someone in the finance team. I'd have to fight for my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should bring it in carefully and keep experienced people to check it. With friends and at the mosque I'd say companies have a duty to the people who built them, not just to shareholders. I'm for business, but I'm also for loyalty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my role gets folded into a bigger one within three years. I'm good but not the best manager at head office, and the ones who'll stay are the ones who learned the new tools first. I'm usually a follower on that, which worries me now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the supply chain analytics course Marlowe offers, the one my colleague Ruth did last year and liked. I'd volunteer my team to test the new planning tool, so we're shaping it rather than being judged by it. And Karim and I would probably wait a year on the baby until I know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can work with it. I'd rather know than not know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait on the baby? Isn't Karim's job steady?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, water pipes don't fix themselves yet. But I don't want to go on maternity leave and come back to a desk that's gone. I'd rather sort my job first, then start the family with my head clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniyal and Joyce, both supporting their parents. Joyce is 49 and has been planning stock for nearly as long as I've been alive. I'd make sure the bosses knew how much she catches that the software misses.

say: Bring it in **carefully** and keep experienced people checking.
Firms have a **duty to the people** who built them, not just shareholders.
think: My role gets **folded into** a bigger one within three years.
I'm usually a **follower** on new tools, which worries me now.
do: Take the **analytics course** on supply chains Marlowe offers.
**Volunteer my team** to test the new planning tool.
Wait **a year** on the baby until my job is clear.
feel: **Anxious**, but I'd **rather know** than not know.
S1.quote: I don't want to go on maternity leave and come back to a desk that's gone.
fieldNote: Planning and buying are **named on the card**, and she knows it means her team.
Her **follower instinct** with technology now feels like a risk.
She'd **delay a baby** to secure her job before maternity leave.
Karim's **hands-on water job** is the household's steady base.

steps.text: Sign up for Marlowe's supply chain analytics course
Volunteer the team to test the new planning tool
Wait a year longer before trying for a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then I think my job's gone, honestly, and most of head office with it. If AI can plan, buy and check, there's nothing my team does that it can't. Karim's job is out on the pipes, so his has a few more years, but mine doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is reckless, and that the government should make companies keep people on for a transition period. At the mosque I'd say families need to pull together. I wouldn't say much at work, because people would be frightened enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be gone within a year of 2028. We'd manage on Karim's salary and our savings, but we'd lose about half our income. And it would change everything about when we have children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month, Karim and I would go through every bill and cut the gym, the second car and our summer trip to see his family. I'd overpay the mortgage while I still had my salary, so it's smaller when I lose it. And I'd look for a job closer to the stores, like regional operations, where you're out visiting shops and dealing with people face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. I'd be lying awake running numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I might go the other way. If my job's going anyway, maybe that's the time to have a child and stay home, and live on Karim's pay for a few years. My mother would say that's what she did, and we turned out fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Karim's job has a few more years. What happens around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up, really. If robots can fix water pipes by 2031, my husband and I would both be out of work within three years of each other. Two years for me, five for him, and a baby in the middle.

say: This is **reckless**; government should make firms keep people for a transition.
Families need to **pull together**, I'd say at the mosque.
think: I'd be **gone within a year** of 2028.
We'd lose **half our income**, living on Karim's salary and savings.
do: **Cut the gym**, the second car and the summer trip.
**Overpay the mortgage** while I still have a salary.
Look for **regional operations** work visiting stores.
S2.quote: If robots can fix water pipes by 2031, my husband and I would both be out of work within three years of each other.
fieldNote: Her job has **no hands-on part**, so 2028 is the date that matters.
She may **flip her baby plans**, having a child sooner and staying home.
The **robot gap** means Karim's job goes soon after hers, which frightens her most.

steps.text: Cut the gym, second car and summer trip to Karim's family
Overpay the mortgage while my salary still comes in
Apply for regional operations roles visiting Marlowe stores
Consider having a baby sooner and staying home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to breathe. I'd be 32 when it lands, maybe with one child. It's still my job that goes, but I'd have time to move somewhere better first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough warning, so there's no excuse for companies or government to be caught out. At work I'd tell my planners to learn something new now. With family I'd say we just need to be sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd get two or three more good years at Marlowe, then the planning team goes. I'm not the kind of manager to jump first, but five years is enough for me to watch what others do and then follow quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the analytics course in year one and then try to move into store operations, the regional manager role that visits 20 shops. That's people work with a hands-on side, so it should last a bit longer. Karim and I would try for a baby in year two, once I'd moved, and keep saving a fifth of what we earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steadier than the fast one. I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch what others do first. Who would you watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, mostly, she's two years ahead of me and always tries things first. If she moved into operations and liked it, I'd follow within the year. That's how I've always done it, and it's worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when robots arrive around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd hope to be the person store managers call when things go wrong, not someone counting stock. Maybe that lasts, maybe not. I'm not going to pretend I know what 2034 looks like.

say: Five years is **enough warning**; nobody should be caught out.
I'd tell my planners to **learn something new** now.
think: I'd get **two or three** good years before the planning team goes.
I'd **watch others first**, then follow quickly.
do: Do the **analytics course** in year one.
Move into **regional store operations**, visiting 20 shops.
Try for a **baby in year two**, after the move.
feel: **Uneasy but steadier**, because I'd have a plan.
S3.quote: I'm not the kind of manager to jump first, but five years is enough for me to watch what others do and then follow quickly.
fieldNote: Her **steady style** works here: she'd follow her colleague Ruth into operations.
She picks **store operations** for its people work and hands-on side.
She **won't guess** about 2034 and says so plainly.

steps.text: Finish Marlowe's analytics course in the first year
Move into a regional store operations role covering 20 shops
Try for a baby in year two, after the move
Keep saving a fifth of our joint income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, that's much easier for us. I'd be 37, probably with two children at school, and Karim and I would have paid off a good chunk of the house. I'd have changed jobs at least once by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is enough time for anyone willing to work at it. I'd encourage the young ones on my team to pick up a trade or something people-facing. And I'd say schools should start teaching children practical skills again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd want to be working part time in store operations, or not at all for a few years while the children are small. Our house would be mostly paid for by 2036, so my family wouldn't need two full salaries when AI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have our first child on our original plan, in about two years. I'd overpay the mortgage by 300 a month so the house is nearly ours by the mid-2030s. And around 2029, I'd move into store operations once I've seen others make the switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly at peace with it. A little worry for Karim further out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why worry for Karim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his robots come about 2039, when he'll be nearly 40 with a family. That's late to start again. I'd want him to move into supervising engineers well before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your children about work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn something with their hands and something with people, both. My father fixed cars and my mother ran a shop, and they always had work. I'd want my children to have that kind of solid footing.

say: Ten years is **enough time** for anyone willing to work.
Young people should pick up **a trade** or people work.
think: I'd be **fine**, with our house **mostly paid for** by 2036.
I might work **part time** while the children are small.
do: Have our **first child** on the original plan.
feel: **Mostly at peace**, with a little worry for **Karim**.
S4.quote: Our house would be mostly paid for by 2036, so my family wouldn't need two full salaries when AI arrives.
fieldNote: With ten years, her **own income** looks safe enough through a paid-off house and Karim's pay.
Her worry moves to **Karim's job** around 2039.
She'd teach her children **hands and people** skills, like her parents had.

steps.text: Have the first child in about two years, as planned
Overpay the mortgage by 300 a month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit both of us within three years, right when we want to start a family. What would help is companies keeping people on for a proper transition, a year or two, and the government backing training that leads to real jobs. I don't want benefits, I want time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. Everyone talks about jobs, but the real question for people my age is whether you can have children with all this going on. For us, the answer depends almost entirely on how much warning we get.

headlineQuote: The real question for people my age is whether you can have children with all this going on.
portrait: Lena is a **replenishment manager**, aged 27, at Marlowe Supermarkets, leading eight planners.
She's married to Karim, a **water company engineer**, and they own a small house.
She's **calm** in AI Plateau, but planning work makes Steady Disruption **anxious**.
Fast AGI **alarms** her because her job and then Karim's could go within three years.
With ten years she feels **mostly at peace**, planning children and a paid-off house.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hitting both jobs just as they start a **family**.
whatWouldHelp: A **transition period** of a year or two from employers.
**Government-backed training** that leads to real jobs, not benefits.
